WITH order_avgs AS (
  SELECT 
    ordersmark,
    AVG(fillcount) as avg_fillcount
  FROM orderexecutions
  GROUP BY ordersmark
),
global_stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(fillcount) as global_avg_fillcount
  FROM orderexecutions
),
above_global AS (
  SELECT 
    oa.ordersmark,
    oa.avg_fillcount,
    oa.avg_fillcount - gs.global_avg_fillcount as margin_vs_global
  FROM order_avgs oa
  CROSS JOIN global_stats gs
  WHERE oa.avg_fillcount > gs.global_avg_fillcount
),
group_stats AS (
  SELECT AVG(avg_fillcount) as group_avg_fillcount
  FROM above_global
),
above_group AS (
  SELECT 
    ag.ordersmark,
    ag.avg_fillcount,
    ag.margin_vs_global,
    ag.avg_fillcount - gs.group_avg_fillcount as margin_vs_group
  FROM above_global ag
  CROSS JOIN group_stats gs
  WHERE ag.avg_fillcount > gs.group_avg_fillcount
)
SELECT
  AVG(avg_fillcount) as avg_fillcount_final,
  AVG(margin_vs_global) as avg_margin_vs_global,
  AVG(margin_vs_group) as avg_margin_vs_group
FROM above_group

assumptions.assumption: The phrase 'average beats the average' interprets 'beats' as strictly greater than (>), not (>=). An order's average must be strictly greater than a benchmark to be retained.
The phrase 'average across all orders' refers to the simple average of all fillcount values across all orderexecutions rows, rather than the average of pre-computed per-order averages.

alternatives.interpretation: The 'average across all orders' could mean the average of per-order averages: compute each order's average fillcount, then average those values to form the global benchmark. This treats the benchmark symmetrically with the values being compared (both are 'order averages').
